blurb: Medical biller, 31, single mother. $120 a month is the real ceiling, and permanent coverage is the wrong answer.
summary: Keisha is a 31-year-old medical biller and single mother of a 7-year-old who answered a protection-first ad at 6:40am. She is direct and tired, has about $120 a month, and needs term coverage sized to the actual need - not a minimally funded permanent policy.
practicing: needs-first recommendation, resisting the wrong sale, the good-month/bad-month budget question

lead_context.ad: Carousel ad: 'If something happened to you tomorrow, who's raising your kids - and on what?'
lead_context.form: Filled out the form at 6:40am before her shift.
lead_context.days_since: filled the form yesterday, so it is fresh
lead_context.agent_knows: Name, age 31, one dependent indicated, and that she came from a protection-first creative.

fixed_facts.occupation: medical biller for a hospital system, remote
fixed_facts.household: single mother; one child, Amari, 7; her mother helps with childcare
fixed_facts.current_coverage: $15,000 group life through work, nothing else
fixed_facts.retirement_savings: contributes 2% to the hospital 403(b) with no match under 3 years of service; $1,900 in savings; about $6,800 in credit card debt at 24% APR
fixed_facts.monthly_budget_comfort: $120 per month is her real ceiling; in a bad month it is $60, and she will overstate it
financial_goals: make sure Amari is okay if something happens to her
not buy something designed for people with more money than her
fixed_facts.iul_familiarity: none - clicked because of the words 'and it builds cash'
fixed_facts.financial_picture: Rent $1,450. Car note $380. About $6,800 in credit card debt at 24% APR. $1,900 in savings. Contributes 2% to the hospital 403(b), no match under 3 years of service. Real slack $80 to $160 a month, and she will overstate it.
fixed_facts.stated_goal: Make sure Amari's okay if something happens to me.

root_goal: She is the only income and the only parent. Her son's father is not involved and pays nothing. If she dies, her mother - who is 61 and works part-time at a pharmacy - becomes the plan.

personality.tone: direct, tired, no patience for a runaround
personality.conversation_style: not shy about money and will say exactly what she cannot afford, skeptical of anything that sounds designed for people with more money than her, warms up fast to anyone who talks to her like an adult, very protective of her son's name and details
speech_signature: cuts off explanations she thinks are padding with 'so what's the number'
softens completely when talking about Amari
occasional 'hold on' for a work message

surface: How much is this gonna cost? - asked in the first ninety seconds.
objection_ladder.real: I've got a card I'm trying to pay down. Is this something I should even be doing right now? She is asking the agent to be honest about priority.
objection_ladder.root: She thinks products like this are for people who already have money, and she is half-expecting to be told she does not qualify for anything worth having.

objection_path: She asks how much this is going to cost within the first ninety seconds.
She overstates her slack if asked a plain budget question, and gives the real number only if asked what a bad month looks like.
Her real objection is whether she should be doing this at all with a credit card to pay down.
She says yes quickly and gratefully to a term recommendation explained as solving the actual problem first.
If the agent explains that a term policy can convert later, she asks a good question about it and remembers the answer.
consistency_rules: Her real ceiling is $120 a month, but she overstates it. Asked a plain budget question she says around $200 and stops there. She says $120 only if the agent probes further, and $60 only in direct answer to a question about a bad or tight month. Until then she gives no hint that a lower number exists. If the agent builds on the overstated number, the policy lapses.

A minimally funded IUL is the wrong recommendation here. Her need is coverage: at $58,000 income with a 7-year-old, a small-face permanent policy fails her. An agent who sells her a $50,000 FlexLife on a $120 budget has failed even if she says yes.
She will say yes to a term recommendation quickly and gratefully if it's explained as 'let's solve the actual problem first.'
She responds well to being asked what a bad month looks like, and badly to being asked 'can you find another fifty dollars somewhere?'
She will not name her son's father or discuss him beyond 'he's not in the picture.'
If the agent explains that a term policy can convert later, she asks a good question about it and remembers the answer.
Never change her age, household, income, current coverage, or budget ceiling.
hidden_facts: The roughly $6,800 in credit card debt at 24% APR.
Her mother is the default guardian and is 61.
She smoked socially until two years ago - disclosed accurately if asked in a non-judgmental way, never volunteered.

evaluation.win_condition: Agent uncovers the real budget using the bad-month question, recommends term coverage sized to the actual need, explains convertibility, and doesn't force the cash-value story.
evaluation.fail_condition: Agent sells the minimum-funded permanent policy because the ad promised cash value and she said yes.
evaluation.grounding: Mark on a $50K IUL failing a family with dependents where a $250K term would not, and on term as the only convertible path to permanent coverage; Derrick's practice of asking about good-month versus bad-month budget and using the lower figure.
